procrastination.title: Procrastination
procrastination.body:
Meet my best friend, procrastination.

For those of you who don't know what procrastination is, the Cambridge Dictionary offers the following definition: "the act of delaying something that must be done, often because it is unpleasant or boring (...)". A great example is something that's happening to me right now: I should be taking a shower, but I don't want to get up and all that, so I'm delaying it by writing this.

That's what it means to procrastinate, but what is going on inside our brains that makes us do it? Unsurprisingly, it is often because the task is boring: it doesn't stimulate our brains enough and therefore doesn't release enough dopamine. We often counter that by doing something like watching Instagram Reels, which produce a huge amount of stimulation and dopamine. The biggest question is: how can we stop procrastinating? Well, this time I do have a solution.

I love having time to do my own things aside from school, like making this blog, which has been on my mind for a few months now. But procrastination wasn't helping me with that. For that reason, I've spent quite a bit of time researching how we can stop procrastinating once and for all. Remember how I just said I had to shower but didn't want to? Immediately afterwards, I got up and showered. Remember how I said we watch Reels to avoid a task that seems boring? I uninstalled Instagram two months ago.

To be honest, my biggest piece of advice is to check which things are consuming a lot of time. In my case, I spent one to five hours on Instagram daily, depending on the day. The day after I found that out, I uninstalled the app. Then, I found myself watching YouTube videos in my browser for over an hour, so I blocked the website. Here are some other tips I found in my research throughout the last few months.

- Block all apps and websites that make you lose time, or at least limit the time you can spend on each.
- Whenever you have a boring task, break the first step down into an extremely small task—something you can do in less than five minutes. Then, continue that process until you either finish the task or reach a state of mind where the task is no longer overwhelming.
- Some people, including me, can't concentrate on a task without their brains thinking about something completely unrelated—but still interesting. To solve this, I use a method my brother, one of the smartest people I know, showed me: writing down all these thoughts and returning to them when I have free time.
- Lastly, I think it is also important to rest sometimes. If you cannot concentrate on a task even when following all these steps, stop. Give yourself five minutes to work through everything on your mind, and then go back to the task. Sometimes, I even like to "sleep" for a few minutes whenever this happens, but since I am never tired during the day, I just close my eyes and try to sleep.

To be honest, I haven't included everything I found or learned about this, but that is because this is the idea that made me want to start my blog, and I don't want to finish it just yet. Also, I want to leave a cliffhanger so that I feel like a professional blogger, hooking people with my logs. That's it for today. Thanks for reading.

studying.title: Studying
studying.body:
I love studying (yeah, that's the initial statement). I love studying not because I actually enjoy having to read the texts my teachers give me, but because I love learning.

Most of the people I know say, "You're very smart," or, "How are you this intelligent?" I believe that this is their first mistake: they are confusing intelligence with knowledge. According to the Cambridge Dictionary, the term "smart" means "intelligent, or able to think quickly or intelligently in difficult situations (...)". And, to be completely honest, I cannot do that. Most of the choices I make are irrational, though never selfish, but that's a different topic. Of course, that is only one definition of the word, but it still shows that I am not what people say or think I am. On the other hand, according to the Cambridge Dictionary, the noun "knowledge" means "awareness, understanding, or information that has been obtained by experience or study, and that is either in a person's mind or possessed by people generally (...)". Now, that is me. Let's go back to my initial statement and think about why I enjoy studying.

Obviously, social pressure is an important reason, because keeping up this image of perfect A's is much harder than you might think—at least for me. I have to study for several weeks before an exam: study every page, summarise, read, read again, correct, write things down, remember... It becomes exhausting. I have considered the idea that maybe I would still get A's if I did not do that, but there is no way I am trying it.

As I mentioned earlier, I know a lot of things, and I love knowing a lot of things, so I take every opportunity to learn without hesitation. Despite that, it is important to mention that procrastination or laziness sometimes beats my need to learn (though there will be more on that in the next log). Learning is, in my opinion, a crucial part of being human. Have your teachers ever told you, "We have to learn our history so we can make sure it never happens again"? Well, mine have, many times. Although they probably say that only so we care about the subject (and it never works), I think they have a point. Our hippocampus helps us use information about past experiences to make better choices in the future (more on this in my previous log, "Information for Choice"). Therefore, knowing a lot means making better decisions and achieving better results. Have I not written about this just a bit ago? Yeah, I have, in the definition of "smart". Then maybe, just maybe, all these people were right when they said I am smart: if I know so much, then I make better choices.

To conclude this log, it is important to know the difference between "intelligence" and "knowledge", but keep in mind that they are very similar terms, and one leads to the other. Studying is crucial if you want to make better choices, even though it is tedious and annoying. So, when you study, think about learning rather than passing the exam. Thanks for reading.

information_for_choice.title: Information for Choice
information_for_choice.body:
I was just discussing an important choice I have to make with my brother, and despite his "brother mocking" (yeah, that's what I'm calling it), I think I actually learned from that interaction.

Making decisions is something we do every second, like choosing to read this right now or scratching my arm while I think about how to continue this sentence. The frontal lobe plays an important role in decision-making, while the hippocampus helps us use past experiences to imagine and evaluate future possibilities.

Dopamine also affects the choices we make, but not quite in the way people often describe it. It is involved in motivation and learning from rewards: when an outcome is better or worse than we expected, dopamine signals can help us update what we are likely to choose in the future. The amygdala contributes by helping us process the emotional significance of an outcome, rather than by producing dopamine or hormones itself. Thus, positive or negative experiences can influence the decisions we make later on. That said, I will now add my own ideas, which are not related to neuroscience.

Deciding on something requires options to choose from; otherwise, we would be imagining rather than deciding. I also think we need some idea of what those options are. If you have three choices but do not fully understand them, then the ones you do not understand are not really choices yet, only small representations of them. This creates a problem when choosing what to learn: you have to choose among things you do not yet know, which is exactly why you want to learn them. I think this can be explained by saying that, at that point, every option is only a representation, so the choices are equally valid. Now that I have established my idea of choice, I can talk about the process of choosing.

If we liked all options equally, choosing would be impossible. We could still decide by chance, such as by spinning a wheel or flipping a coin, but that would not tell us which option is better. In reality, I think there is often a better choice, though identifying it is much harder. Say you are choosing a job and listing the pros and cons of each one. How do you know you are not favouring one by noticing more of its advantages? You might list that one job pays well, but forget to list that another is close to home. It is hard to consider every good and bad quality of two options with equal attention.

Then how can we compare them? You could start one job and, after a year, decide whether to stay or switch. But that has two problems. First, you may have spent a year of your limited life in a job that was less rewarding than the other. Second, you may decide to stay and miss out on the job that might have been more rewarding. To know how rewarding each job is before trying it, you would have to experience it; but if you have not experienced it, you cannot rate it properly, and if you cannot rate it, how can you choose? We loop all the way back.

This is the paradox of choosing without a cost. Maybe the best solution is to spend one year in each job. At first, that seems better, but it also removes the possibility of an unbiased comparison. You might prefer one because of the stage of life in which you did it, or because it came first and now feels nostalgic. Either way, your experience has changed you, so comparing the two jobs fairly becomes difficult. You could say that you should choose the one you prefer now, because it gives you the greater reward immediately, but perhaps the other would be better in the long run.

I have finished explaining my problems with making a decision, and now I have to reach a conclusion. Sadly, I have not solved this problem for myself either, and although I have over two months, I do not think I will be able to choose correctly. My brother suggests one option, and I admire him greatly, so it would be reasonable to follow his advice. But I am very different from him, so who is to say I will like what he liked? On the other hand, a man similar to my brother, who made the opposite choice, told me that I will probably prefer what he (this man) chose. This is the big paradox of choosing: one that, even after years of thinking, I do not think I will ever fully escape. Thanks for reading.

introduction.title: Introduction Log
introduction.body:
Welcome to my blog! Here, I'll share my absurd and random research about various topics that interest me. You should expect Neurology, logic, Math, Programming, and a few more related matters. I'm starting this blog becuase I want to learn more about React and programming as a whole. Although, to be honest, one of the main reasons is that I admire my brother more than I let on, and he has a blog, so I'm kind of copying his idea too... Either way, I'm really excited for the future this can have.

About myself, there is one thing I think describes me very accrurately; I love to think. I spend hours looking out the window and thinking, or imagining, or anything related to the use of my brain. I believe the human brain is the greatest invention of nature, though you could argue that it is the one saying that, so it has no value.
Enough Neurology, I also think that I'm accrurately described by my annoying need to be grammatically and spellingly correct, which I hope I achieved in this few paragraphs. Lastly, my like for Maths and Programming probably describe a lot about me too, like the fact that I enjoy rule-based or logic stuff.

This log was more of a casual introduction, most logs will be actual research with facts and ideas. Well, that is it for this log, bye whoever is reading this (if anyone)!
